settings.description: The address and port Keystone listens on. The default is reachable from this machine only.
Whether the session cookie is marked for HTTPS only. Turn it on once Keystone is reached over HTTPS. A request that arrives over HTTPS gets the mark whatever this says.
The most bytes the API reads from one request's body. A larger body is refused.
How often an open stream sends a line that means only that it is still there, so nothing between Keystone and the browser closes a quiet connection.
The most rows a list in the API returns in one call. A client reads further pages to get the rest.
Whether the API tells someone who has not signed in the names of the people on this install, so the sign-in screen can ask who is signing in. Off, a person must know their own id.

How many rounds of PBKDF2-SHA-256 a password goes through before it is stored. More rounds make a stolen database slower to guess from. A stored password moves to the new count the next time its person signs in.
The fewest characters a new password may have.
How long a sign-in lasts before the person must sign in again.
How many wrong passwords in a row are taken before password sign-in makes the person wait.
How long password sign-in is refused after too many wrong passwords in a row.
Whether people may add passkeys and sign in with them. Off until the sign-in screen has proven them in a browser.
The host name passkeys are bound to, which must be the host people reach Keystone by. Changing it makes every stored passkey unusable.
The address in the browser's bar when a passkey is used: scheme, host and port. A passkey answer from any other page is refused.
How long a person has to answer a passkey prompt before it must be asked again.

Whether rebuild loads the test tenant into the data folder: an invented person whose password is published in the repo, with a few chats and the fake provider for a model. Switch it off on an install that people outside the home can reach.

How many rounds of PBKDF2-SHA-256 turn a backup's passphrase into its key, from 100000 to 50000000. More rounds make a stolen backup slower to guess from. A backup records its own count, so a change applies to the next backup only.
The fewest characters a backup's passphrase may have.
The period the usage report shows when none is asked for: this month, last month, or the last 7 or 30 days, in calendar days in UTC as the monthly cap counts them.
How many lines each breakdown of the usage report shows, by model, by chat and by kind of work, costliest first, before the rest are added up in one more line. Below 1 is taken as 1.
The most days one usage report may cover when it is asked for a range of days.

How often the server records where each person's limits stand (the monthly cap, the memory reserve, the disk, their database, files and artifacts), so Operations can show each limit's trend. From 1m to 24h.
How long a snapshot of a limit is kept before it is removed. 840h is 35 days.
The size, in megabytes, a person's database (keystone.db with its write-ahead log) is planned to grow to. Operations shows the database against it.
The room, in megabytes, set for one person's files folder: uploads and project files. Operations shows the folder against it.
The room, in megabytes, set for one person's artifacts folder. Operations shows the folder against it.

How far back Operations looks to tell each limit's trend: its growth a day and when it would fill at that rate. 168h is a week; the monthly cap and the memory reserve look back no further than the start of the month.
The recent window Operations reads each model's calls, errors, refusals and median time over, and the background tasks that failed.
How many of the newest background tasks and scheduled runs Operations lists, and how many of those that failed. From 1 to 100.
How many of the newest traces Operations lists: each turn or run with its calls, tool steps, tokens, cost and outcome. From 1 to 100.
A background task or scheduled run whose round has gone on longer than this, and is not paused or waiting for your approval, is listed as stuck on Operations.
The share of a model's calls in the health window, in percent, that may fail before Operations shows the model as having errors.
How full the volume that holds Keystone's data folder may get, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you.
How much of its planned size your database may reach, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you.
How much of its room your files folder may use, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you.
How much of its room your artifacts folder may use, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you.
How much of the memory pass's reserve may be spent in a month, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you. The monthly cap's own level is usage.cap_warn_percent.
How much of its own budget a background task or scheduled run under way may spend, in percent, before Operations and the home screen tell you.
The folder that holds keystone.json and one folder for each tenant.

Where a new install keeps the master key that protects every tenant's secrets. system is the operating system's key store: DPAPI on Windows, the login keychain on macOS, the Secret Service on Linux. file is a key file in the user's profile, for a machine with no key store, and is weaker. Once an install has stored a secret, keystone.json records the keeper and this setting is no longer read.
